structured_output.hypothesis: If Darwin's claim holds, the radiometrically calibrated numeric age of the end of the Chalk (the latest Cretaceous, the late Secondary) is at least about 300 million years, because denudation of the Weald began only after the Chalk was deposited.
structured_output.pass_criterion: The International Chronostratigraphic Chart gives the top of the Cretaceous (the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, which ends the Chalk) an age of 270 Ma or older, so that 'far more than 300 Myr' is at least approximately supported.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The chart gives the top of the Cretaceous an age younger than 150 Ma. The current value is about 66.0 Ma, so Darwin's figure is overestimated by a factor of at least 2. An age between 150 and 270 Ma is inconclusive and counts as not confirmed.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' is the Late Cretaceous, when the Chalk was deposited. Only the time from the end of Chalk deposition to the present is available for denudation of the Weald. Darwin's figure came from an assumed erosion rate of 1 inch per century, applied to a cliff 500 ft high that retreated about 22 miles. The test is a modern reinterpretation. It does not re-derive the rate. It compares his implied elapsed time, 300 Myr, with the independently dated age of the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary. That age is the upper bound on time available for the Weald's denudation. The Weald's anticline was uplifted and eroded in the Cenozoic, so the real time available is shorter still. A result of about 66 Ma refutes the 300 Myr figure. The qualitative claim that geological time is very long survives, because 66 Myr is still vast.

dataset.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart
dataset.why_it_fits: The chart gives numeric boundary ages in Ma for every stage and system, and is available as downloadable PDF and image files. The field used is the numeric age of the top of the Cretaceous System, the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, with the Maastrichtian and Campanian stages for the Chalk. The age is compared against Darwin's 300 Myr.
